1 # `A2G2` Linear Subdivision 2 3 Unlike most other global remeshing operations, linear (and Catmull-Clark) subdivision will proceed by completely replacing the original halfedge mesh with a new one. The high-level procedure is: 4 5 1. Generate a list of vertex positions for the new mesh. 6 2. Generate a list of polygons for the new mesh, as a list of indices into the new vertex list (a la "polygon soup"). 7 3. Using these two lists, rebuild the halfedge connectivity from scratch. 8 9 Given these lists, `Halfedge_Mesh::from_poly` will take care of allocating halfedges, setting up `next` and `twin` pointers, etc., based on the list of polygons generated in step $2$---this routine is already implemented in the Scotty3D skeleton code. 10 11 Both linear and Catmull-Clark subdivision schemes will handle general $n$-gons (i.e., polygons with $n$ sides) rather than, say, quads only or triangles only. Each $n$-gon (including but not limited to quadrilaterals) will be split into $n$ quadrilaterals according to the following template: 12 13

14 15 The high-level procedure is outlined in greater detail in `student/meshedit.cpp`. 16 17 ### Vertex Positions 18 19 For global linear or Catmull-Clark subdivision, the strategy for assigning new vertex positions may at first appear a bit strange: in addition to updating positions at vertices, we will also calculate vertex positions associated with the _edges_ and _faces_ of the original mesh. Storing new vertex positions on edges and faces will make it extremely convenient to generate the polygons in our new mesh, since we can still use the halfedge data structure to decide which four positions get connected up to form a quadrilateral. In particular, each quad in the new mesh will consist of: 20 21 * One new vertex associated with a face from the original mesh, 22 * Two new vertices associated with edges from the original mesh, and 23 * One vertex from the original mesh. 24 25 For linear subdivision, the rules for computing new vertex positions are very simple: 26 27 * New vertices at original faces are assigned the average coordinates of all corners of that face (i.e., the arithmetic mean). 28 * New vertices at original edges are assigned the average coordinates of the two edge endpoints. 29 * New vertices at original vertices are assigned the same coordinates as in the original mesh. 30 31 These values should be assigned to the members `Face::new_pos`, `Edge::new_pos`, and `Vertex::new_pos`, respectively. For instance, `f->new_pos = Vec3( x, y, z );` will assign the coordinates $(x,y,z)$ to the new vertex associated with face $f$. The general strategy for assigning these new positions is to iterate over all vertices, then all edges, then all faces, assigning appropriate values to `new_pos`. **Note:** you _must_ copy the original vertex position `Vertex::pos` to the new vertex position `Vertex::new_pos`; these values will not be used automatically. 32 33 This step should be implemented in the method `Halfedge_Mesh::linear_subdivide_positions` in `student/meshedit.cpp`. 34 35 Steps $2$ and $3$ are already implemented by `Halfedge_Mesh::subdivide` in `geometry/halfedge.cpp`. For your understanding, an explanation of how these are implemented is provided below: 36 37 ### Polygons 38 39 Recall that in linear and Catmull-Clark subdivision _all polygons are subdivided simultaneously_. In other words, if we focus on the whole mesh (rather than a single polygon), then we are globally 40 41 * Creating one new vertex for each edge, 42 * Creating one new vertex for each face, and 43 * Keeping all the vertices of the original mesh. 44 45 These vertices are then connected up to form quadrilaterals (_n_ quadrilaterals for each _n_-gon in the input mesh). Rather than directly modifying the halfedge connectivity, these new quads will be collected in a much simpler mesh data structure: a list of polygons. Note that with this subdivision scheme, _every_ polygon in the output mesh will be a quadrilateral, even if the input contains triangles, pentagons, etc. 46 47 In Scotty3D, a list of polygons can be declared as 48 49 ```cpp 50 std::vector> quads; 51 ``` 52 53 where `std::vector` is a [class from the C++ standard template library](http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector), representing a dynamically-sized array. An `Index` is just another name for a `size_t`, which is the standard C++ type for integers that specify an element of an array. Polygons can be created by allocating a list of appropriate size, then specifying the indices of each vertex in the polygon. For example: 54 55 ```cpp 56 std::vector quad( 4 ); // allocate an array with four elements 57 // Build a quad with vertices specified by integers (a,b,c,d), starting at zero. 58 // These indices should correspond to the indices computing when assigning vertex 59 // positions, as described above. 60 quad[0] = a; 61 quad[1] = b; 62 quad[2] = c; 63 quad[3] = d; 64 ``` 65 66 Once a quad has been created, it can be added to the list of quads by using the method `vector::push_back`, which appends an item to a vector: 67 68 ```cpp 69 std::vector> newPolygons; 70 newPolygons.push_back( quad ); 71 ``` 72 73 The full array of new polygons will then be passed to the method `Halfedge_Mesh::from_poly`, together with the new vertex positions. 74

1	# `A2G3` Catmull-Clark Subdivision
2	
3	The only difference between Catmull-Clark and [linear](linear.md) subdivision is the choice of positions for new vertices. Whereas linear subdivision simply takes a uniform average of the old vertex positions, Catmull-Clark uses a very carefully-designed _weighted_ average to ensure that the surface converges to a nice, round surface as the number of subdivision steps increases. The original scheme is described in the paper _"Recursively generated B-spline surfaces on arbitrary topological meshes"_ by (Pixar co-founder) Ed Catmull and James Clark. Since then, the scheme has been thoroughly discussed, extended, and analyzed; more modern descriptions of the algorithm may be easier to read, including those from the [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catmull-Clark_subdivision_surface) and [this webpage](http://www.rorydriscoll.com/2008/08/01/catmull-clark-subdivision-the-basics/). In short, the new vertex positions can be calculated by:
4	
5	1.  Setting the new vertex position at each face $f$ to the average of all its original vertices (exactly as in linear subdivision),
6	2.  Setting the new vertex position at each edge $e$ to the average of the new adjacent face positions (from step 1) **and** the original edge endpoint positions, and
7	3.  Setting the new vertex position at each vertex $v$ to the weighted sum
8	
9	
10	$$\frac{Q+2R+(n-3)S}{n}$$
11	
12	
13	where $n$ is the degree of vertex $v$ (i.e., the number of faces containing $v$), and
14	
15	*   $Q$ is the average of all new face position for faces containing $v$,
16	*   $R$ is the average of all original edge midpoints for edges containing $v$, and
17	*   $S$ is the original vertex position for vertex $v$.
18	
19	In other words, the new vertex positions are an "average of averages." (Note that you _will_ need to divide by $n$ _both_ when computing $Q$ and $R$, _and_ when computing the final, weighted value---this is not a typo!)
20	
21	### Boundaries
22	For the boundary case, we want to handle it similar to how it's outlined [here](http://15462.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2022/lecture/geometryprocessing/slide_023). The idea is to make it have the same behavior as if the object had been cut in half at that face.
23	
24	If we take a look at what this means for boundary edges, we see that we would normally average the two adjacent face points along with the two adjacent vertices forming this edge. Since we mirrored the shape to create one of these face points, the average of the two face points will end up becoming the midpoint of the original edge. Averaging the midpoint of the original edge with the midpoint will result in the midpoint.
25	
26	For boundary vertices, we can think of it in a similar way. The face average would end up becoming some average of the original vertex and the neighboring vertices on the boundary face, while the edge average would end up with something similar. The math here ends up working out to a weighting of $$\frac{3}{4}$$ on the original vertex and $$\frac{1}{8}$$ on the neighboring boundary vertices.

1 # All About `Halfedge_Mesh` 2 3 In our code, a halfedge mesh -- represented by the `Halfedge_Mesh` structure -- is a pointer-based repository for manifold mesh connectivity and data. 4 This section provides an overview of some key ideas about halfedge meshes and the `Halfedge_Mesh` structure in particular. Consider it a supplement to a thorough reading of `src/geometry/halfedge.h`. 5 6 ## Mesh Elements and Memory Management 7 8 A `Halfedge_Mesh` wrangles four mesh element types: `Vertices`, `Edges`, `Faces`, and `Halfedges`: 9 10 11 12 As a pointer-based structure, `Halfedge_Mesh` operations will often require the allocation and deallocation of new elements. Rather than using the C++ `new` and `delete` operators directly, `Halfedge_Mesh` instead provides `emplace_*` and `erase_*` functions to allocate and free (respectively) mesh elements. This allows the mesh to track all of the elements that belong to it in `std::list`s (called `vertices`, `edges`, `faces`, and `halfedges`). 13 14 The functions also maintain a unique-within-the-mesh `id` value for mesh elements, which can be useful for debugging (printing `v->id` for debug messages is a lot more readable than `&*v`). As an additional feature, the high-order bit of the `id` is set by the `erase_*` functions. So if you start seeing very very large id values, you probably have a use-after-free bug. 15 16 ## Mesh Connectivity 17 18 In our halfedge mesh structure, elements store both connectivity information as references (really, `std::list< >` iterators) to other elements. 19 20 Vertices store a reference to one of the halfedges directed away from them in `Vertex::halfedge`: 21 22 23 24 Edges store a reference to one of the halfedges that make them up in `Edge::halfedge`: 25 26 27 28 Faces store a reference to one of the halfedges that circulate around them in `Face::halfedge`: 29 30 31 32 Halfedges store the bulk of the connectivity information. They store a reference to the halfedge on the other side of their edge in `Halfedge::twin`, a reference to the halfedge that follows them in their current face in `Halfedge::next`, a reference to the vertex they leave in `Halfedge::vertex`, a reference to the edge they border in `Halfedge::edge`, and a reference to the face they circulate in `Halfedge::face`: 33 34 35 36 ## Mesh Data 37 38 In addition to the mesh connectivity, the mesh stores data on each of the mesh features. 39 40 41 42 Vertices store their location in `position`, and information about skinning (A4!) in `bone_weights`. 43 44 Edges store a `sharp` flag which is used in shading normal computation. If this flag is true, then we treat this edge as a break in the surface when computing shading normals, and if it's false, then we treat this edge as connected when computing shading normals. 45 46 Faces store a `boundary` flag which tells you if the face is a solid face or a face that exists to book-keep holes in the model: 47 48 49 50 Halfedges store `corner_uv` and `corner_normal` values, which are used to set texture coordinates and shading normals for the corner of the face associated with the halfedge. 51 52 53 ### Splitting and Merging Data 54 55 Since it is often the case that you are adding or removing features from the mesh, we include an overloaded `interpolate_data` helper function to help in interpolating/merging `Vertex::bone_weights` and `Halfedge::corner_*` data. (Handling of `Edge::sharp` is probably either obvious [as in splits] or arbitrary [as in merges with different flags]. Handling of `Face::boundary` is generally specified by the operation.) 56 57 Check the comments near `interpolate_data` in `halfedge.h` for some usage examples. 58 59 ## Iterating over the Data 60 61 Down below are some examples of how to iterate using a `Halfedge_Mesh`. Suppose we have a face $f$ and want to print out the positions of all its vertices. We would write a routine like this: 62 63 ``` 64 void printVertexPositions(FaceRef f) { 65 HalfedgeRef h = f->halfedge; // get the first halfedge of the face 66 do { 67 VertexRef v = h->vertex; // get the vertex of the current halfedge 68 std::cout << v->position << std::endl; // print the vertex position 69 h = h->next; // move to the next halfedge around the face 70 } while (h != f->halfedge); // keep going until we're back at the beginning 71 } 72 ``` 73 74 Notice that we refer to a face as a FaceRef rather than just a Face. You can think of a Ref as a kind of pointer. Note that members of an iterator are accessed with an arrow -> rather than a dot ., just as with pointers. (A more in-depth explanation of some of these details can be found in the inline documentation.) Similarly, to print out the positions of all the neighbors of a given vertex we could write a routine like this: 75 76 ``` 77 void printNeighborPositions(VertexRef v) { 78 HalfedgeRef h = v->halfedge; // get one of the outgoing halfedges of the vertex 79 do { 80 HalfedgeRef h_twin = h->twin; // get the vertex of the current halfedge 81 VertexRef vN = h_twin->vertex; // vertex is 'source' of the half edge. 82 // so h->vertex is v, 83 // whereas h_twin->vertex is the neighbor vertex. 84 std::cout << vN->position << std::endl; // print the vertex position 85 h = h_twin->next; // move to the next outgoing halfedge of the vertex. 86 } while(h != v->halfedge); // keep going until we're back at the beginning 87 } 88 ``` 89 90 To iterate over all the vertices in a halfedge mesh, we could write a loop like this: 91 92 ``` 93 for(VertexRef v = vertices_begin(); v != vertices_end(); v++) { 94 printNeighborPositions(v); // do something interesting here 95 } 96 ``` 97 98 ## Temporary Storage 99 100 Sometimes it is useful to associate temporary storage with the various mesh elements. E.g., to store a position or flag on a mesh element during an algorithm. You can use the fact that mesh elements have stable addresses (and we provide a `std::hash` specialization that hashes their addresses) to do this: 101 ```cpp 102 std::unordered_map< VertexRef, Vec3 > next_position; //store data per-element 103 std::unordered_set< VertexRef > was_special; //store a set of VertexRefs 104 105 for (VertexRef v = vertices.begin(); v != vertices.end(); ++v) { 106 next_position[v] = Vec3(0.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f); 107 if (check_something(v)) { 108 was_special.emplace(v); 109 } 110 } 111 112 //... later ... 113 114 for (VertexRef v = vertices.begin(); v != vertices.end(); ++v) { 115 v->position = next_position.at(v); 116 if (was_special.count(v)) { 117 //... 118 } 119 } 120 ``` 121 122 Keep in mind that neither addresses or the order of iteration of hashed containers (`unordered_*`) will be stable between OS's, standard library versions, or even (if using address-space layout randomization) runs of the same program. This probably won't matter for you, but I'm mentioning it now just in case. 123 124 ## Validity 125 126 A `Halfedge_Mesh` structure is a sea of pointers. It is surprisingly easy to tangle these pointers into a mess that fails to represent a manifold mesh (or, really, a consistent mesh at all). In order to provide guidance on what constitutes a reasonable setting for a mesh, we define a *valid* mesh as one for which the following properties hold: 127 1. The mesh is self-contained. All pointers are to elements in the vertices, edges, faces, or halfedges lists. 128 2. Edges correspond to twinned halfedges. That is, for every edge `e`, `e->halfedge(->twin)^n` is a cycle of exactly two halfedges, and these are exactly the halfedges with `h->edge` equal to `e`. 129 3. Faces correspond to cycles of halfedges. That is, for every face `f`, `f->halfedge(->next)^n` is a cycle of at least three halfedges, and these are exactly the halfedges with `h->face` equal to `f`. 130 4. Vertices correspond to stars of halfedges. That is, for every vertex `v`, `v->halfedge(->twin->next)^n` is a cycle of at least two halfedges, and these are exactly the halfedges with `h->vertex` equal to `v`. 131 5. Vertices are not orphaned, nor is the surface adjacent to them hourglass-shaped. That is, vertices are adjacent to at least one non-boundary face and at most one boundary face. 132 6. Edges not orphaned. That is, edges are adjacent to at least one non-boundary face. 133 7. Faces are simple. That is, faces touch each vertex and edge at most once. 134 135 These properties are checked by the `Halfedge_Mesh::validate()` function, which returns `nullopt` if the mesh is valid or an element reference and an explanatory message if something is wrong with the mesh. 136

## 1. What the helper is, exactly

Declared at `/workspace/src/geometry/halfedge.h:182-189`:

```cpp
	//helper for Catmull-Clark-style subdivision.
	// generates topology itself, assigns positions from parameters.
	// used by linear_subdivide and catmark_subdivide.
	void catmark_subdivide_helper(
		std::unordered_map< VertexCRef, Vec3 > const &vertex_positions, //where to move current vertices after subdividing
		std::unordered_map< EdgeCRef, Vec3 > const &edge_vertex_positions, //where to place the center-of-edge vertices
		std::unordered_map< FaceCRef, Vec3 > const &face_vertex_positions //where to place the center-of-face vertices
	);
```

Stub at `/workspace/src/geometry/halfedge-global.cpp:285-300`:

```cpp
/*
 * catmark_subdivide_helper: add vertex in every edge and non-boundary face, set positions from parameters
 *
 * Works on all valid meshes.
 */
void Halfedge_Mesh::catmark_subdivide_helper(
	std::unordered_map< VertexCRef, Vec3 > const &vertex_positions, //positions for vertices after subdivision
	std::unordered_map< EdgeCRef, Vec3 > const &edge_vertex_positions, //positions for new vertices added in each edge
	std::unordered_map< FaceCRef, Vec3 > const &face_vertex_positions //positions for new vertices added in each face
	) {
```

`/workspace/requirements/catmark_subdivide_helper.yaml` states the same: *"split every edge (same concept as `split_edge` applied to all edges), split every non-boundary face into quads around a newly-inserted face-center vertex, then update all vertex positions from pre-computed position maps."*

The only two callers are `linear_subdivide` / `catmark_subdivide` (`halfedge-global.cpp:49` and `:82`) plus the GUI (`/workspace/src/gui/model.cpp:791,794`). The caller decides *geometry only*; the helper owns *all topology*.

## 2. Required topology

**Every edge (interior AND boundary) is split exactly once.** One new vertex per edge; the original edge becomes two edges sharing that vertex. Note `validate()` guarantees no edge has boundary faces on both sides (`halfedge-utility.cpp:642`: `" is orphaned (has no adjacent non-boundary face)."`), so every edge vertex is incident to at least one face center.

**Every non-boundary face `f` of degree `d`:** gets exactly one new center vertex and is replaced by `d` quads, one per original corner. In CCW order each quad is

`(v, midpoint of v's outgoing edge, face center, midpoint of v's incoming edge)`

so `d` new "spoke" edges (edge-vertex → center) and `d-1` net new faces are created.

**Every BOUNDARY face (boundary loop):**
- gets **NO** center vertex,
- is **NOT** split into multiple faces — it stays exactly one face with `boundary == true`,
- its edges *are* split (they are the same edges as the adjacent interior faces'), so its halfedge cycle simply grows from `d` to `2d` halfedges, alternating original vertices and edge-split vertices,
- no new edges are added inside it; the loop remains a single `next`-cycle.

This is pinned down by the tests. `/workspace/tests/a2/test.a2.g2.cpp:28-43` (identical logic in `test.a2.g3.cpp:29-44`):

```cpp
	// check that all faces are degree 4
	for (Halfedge_Mesh::FaceRef f = mesh.faces.begin(); f != mesh.faces.end(); f++) {
		if (!f->boundary && f->degree() != 4) {
			throw Test::error("Linear subdivision created a non-quad face!");
		}
	}

	// check for expected number of elements
	if (numVerts + numEdges + numFaces - mesh.n_boundaries() != mesh.vertices.size()) {
	...
	if (numEdges * 2 + ce != mesh.edges.size()) {
	...
	if (numFaces + cf != mesh.faces.size()) {
```
with `ce`/`cf` accumulated *before* the call over non-boundary faces only (`test.a2.g2.cpp:13-20`):
```cpp
	size_t ce = 0;
	size_t cf = 0;
	for (Halfedge_Mesh::FaceRef f = mesh.faces.begin(); f != mesh.faces.end(); f++) {
		if (!f->boundary) {
			ce += f->degree();
			cf += f->degree() - 1;
		}
	}
```

Rewriting (`numFaces` includes boundary loops, `n_boundaries()` is sampled **after** subdivision):
- `V' = V + E + F_all - B` → one vertex per edge + one per *non-boundary* face; **B must be unchanged**, so boundary loops must neither disappear, multiply, nor become non-boundary.
- `E' = 2E + Σ_{f non-boundary} deg(f)`
- `F' = F_all + Σ_{f non-boundary}(deg(f) - 1)` = `B + Σ_{f non-boundary} deg(f)` → each boundary loop contributes exactly 1 face.
- `H' = 2E'`; degree-4 check exempts boundary faces, which end at degree `2d`.

Structural invariants that `validate()` will enforce on the result (`/workspace/src/geometry/halfedge-utility.cpp:447-663`): face cycles ≥ 3 halfedges; vertex cycles ≥ 2; `v->halfedge`, `e->halfedge`, `f->halfedge` must be halfedges that actually reference them; each vertex on ≤ 1 boundary face and ≥ 1 non-boundary face; faces simple; all `position`/`corner_uv`/`corner_normal` finite.

## 3. Positions: which map feeds which vertex

- **Surviving original vertex `v`** → `vertex_positions[v]`, keyed by the *original* `VertexCRef`. Applies to boundary vertices too (in `a2.g3.catmull_clark.edge.square` the corners move from `(-1,1,0)` to `(-0.75,0.75,0)`).
- **New edge vertex for edge `e`** → `edge_vertex_positions[e]`, for boundary edges as well.
- **New face-center vertex for non-boundary face `f`** → `face_vertex_positions[f]`.
- **Boundary faces are never looked up** — and must not be, because the caller never fills them. `halfedge-global.cpp:42-43`: `// For every *non-boundary* face, assign the centroid (i.e., arithmetic mean) to face_vertex_positions[f]:`. Using `face_vertex_positions.at(f)` over all faces would throw `std::out_of_range` on the square tests.

**Missing entries:** never use `.at()` blindly. Use `find()`/`count()` and degrade gracefully, computing fallbacks from the **pre-subdivision** geometry:
- vertex missing → leave `v->position` unchanged,
- edge missing → `e->center()` (`halfedge-utility.cpp:305`, midpoint of the two endpoints),
- non-boundary face missing → `f->center()` (`halfedge-utility.cpp:309`, centroid of its corners).

This makes an unspecified element behave as plain linear subdivision, keeps every position finite (otherwise `validate()` reports `"has position.x set to a non-finite value"`), and avoids leaving two vertices at `(0,0,0)`, which `Test::differs` rejects up front with `"Source mesh does not have epsilon-unique vertex positions."` (`/workspace/src/test.cpp:465-489`, `epsilon = 0.001f`).

Nothing else is checked geometrically: `Test::differs(Halfedge_Mesh, Halfedge_Mesh)` matches vertices by quantized position, edges by endpoint pairs, faces by **unordered** vertex multiset plus `match->boundary == f->boundary`; corner/uv/sharp data is ignored (`/workspace/src/test.cpp:465`: `//NOTE: check_extra actually ignored for now. Will update!`). Still, good practice: split halves inherit `Edge::sharp`, spokes are non-sharp, and new vertices/halfedges get `interpolate_data({v1,v2}, vm)` / `interpolate_data({h1..hN}, h)` (`halfedge.h:325-345`).

## 4. Worked example — `a2.g2.linear.edge.square` (`/workspace/tests/a2/test.a2.g2.cpp:56-79`)

Input:
```cpp
	Halfedge_Mesh mesh = Halfedge_Mesh::from_indexed_faces({	
		Vec3{-0.5f, 0.0f,-0.5f}, Vec3{-0.5f, 0.0f, 0.5f},
		Vec3{ 0.5f, 0.0f,-0.5f}, Vec3{ 0.5f, 0.0f, 0.5f}
	},{
		{1, 3, 2, 0}
	});
```
`from_indexed_faces` (`/workspace/src/geometry/halfedge-utility.cpp:733-865`) builds:
- V = 4: `v0(-0.5,0,-0.5) v1(-0.5,0,0.5) v2(0.5,0,-0.5) v3(0.5,0,0.5)`
- E = 4: `{v1,v3} {v3,v2} {v2,v0} {v0,v1}`
- F = 2: interior `F0 = v1→v3→v2→v0`; boundary loop `B = v0→v2→v3→v1` (auto-generated from the untwinned halfedges; the `while (!next_on_boundary.empty())` block starts at the smallest index, so the concrete order is `0,2,3,1`)
- H = 8, `n_boundaries() == 1`.

Maps supplied by `linear_subdivide`: 4 vertex entries (identity), 4 edge entries (midpoints), **1** face entry (`F0` → `(0,0,0)`); nothing for `B`.

Expected output (test's `after`, 9 verts / 4 quads, plus the auto boundary loop):

| after idx | position | role |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | (0,0,0) | center of `F0` |
| 1 | (0,0,0.5) | mid `{v1,v3}` |
| 2 | (0.5,0,0.5) | `v3` |
| 3 | (0.5,0,0) | mid `{v3,v2}` |
| 4 | (0.5,0,-0.5) | `v2` |
| 5 | (0,0,-0.5) | mid `{v2,v0}` |
| 6 | (-0.5,0,-0.5) | `v0` |
| 7 | (-0.5,0,0) | mid `{v0,v1}` |
| 8 | (-0.5,0,0.5) | `v1` |

## 5. Ordering / iteration hazards

1. **New elements are appended to the live lists.** `halfedge.h:349-351`: `//use emplace_* to allocate new mesh elements: // elements are added at the end of their respective list`. A loop `for (EdgeRef e = edges.begin(); e != edges.end(); ++e)` will therefore also visit the halves you just created (splitting them again → runaway loop / wrong counts); same for `faces` (new quads) and `vertices`. Snapshot first into `std::vector<EdgeRef>` / `std::vector<FaceRef>`. `std::list` iterators stay valid across insertion and across erasure of *other* nodes, so stored `Ref`s are safe. Saving `edges.end()` as a sentinel does **not** work — new nodes are inserted before `end()`.
2. **Face corner data must be captured before edge splitting.** After all edges are split, an original face's `next`-cycle has `2d` halfedges alternating old/edge vertices; `f->degree()` returns `2d`, and `f->center()` would average 2d points. Either record each face's corner list / centroid fallback first, or knowingly walk the doubled cycle (`h`, `h->next->next`, …).
3. **Positions must be read/derived before any position is written.** Fallback `e->center()` / `f->center()` use `Vertex::position` of the current mesh; if you first write `vertex_positions` into the original vertices, every fallback is computed on the wrong geometry. Compute all new `Vec3`s first, then apply.
4. **Erase + emplace aliases addresses, and the maps hash by address.** `emplace_vertex` recycles: `vertices.splice(vertices.end(), free_vertices, free_vertices.begin());` (`halfedge-utility.cpp:56`, same pattern for edges/faces/halfedges), while `erase_*` only splices into the free list — the object keeps its address. `halfedge.h:517-533` hashes `&*key` (`HASH_BY_ADDRESS`). So an erased-then-reallocated element can silently collide with a live key in `vertex_positions`/`edge_vertex_positions`/`face_vertex_positions`, or make a stale `Ref` point at a *different* live element. The clean route is purely additive: reuse the original faces as one of the quads, the original halfedges as the "first halves", and erase nothing.
5. **Do not drive topology by iterating the `unordered_map`s.** `/workspace/assignments/A2/halfedge.md:122`: *"neither addresses or the order of iteration of hashed containers (`unordered_*`) will be stable between OS's, standard library versions, or even ... runs of the same program."* Iterate the mesh lists; use the maps only for lookup.
6. **Rebuild-from-scratch variant** (`*this = Halfedge_Mesh::from_indexed_faces(new_verts, quads);`, matching the older `from_poly` description in `/workspace/assignments/A2/linear.md`) works and auto-regenerates one boundary loop per original boundary loop with doubled degree — but you must extract every `Vec3` out of the maps *before* the move-assignment, since all map keys are iterators into the mesh you are about to destroy. It also drops `bone_weights`, `Edge::sharp`, `corner_uv`, `corner_normal`, and all element ids, and it `assert`s / silently skips loops with repeated adjacent indices.
7. **Pointer hygiene after splitting:** if the original halfedge becomes the *second* half of a split edge, `v->halfedge` for its origin vertex must be repointed (validate: `"has halfedge(->twin->next)^n which is not a cycle"` / `"is referenced by ... which is not in halfedge(->twin->next)^n"`); likewise re-point `e->halfedge` for the reused edge and `f->halfedge` for reused faces, and set `boundary` correctly on any face you create (all new quads: `false`).
